To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the absence of IL-4 protects against the development of intestinal inflammation and weight loss in food allergy.
lack of IL4 protects from intestinal damage in food allergy by modulating Th1/Th2 responses, and that the intestinal mucosa is an important player in food allergy.

the lack of IL-2/IL-2R signaling in the gut mucosal immune system is sufficient to prevent the development of intestinal inflammation in a murine model of food allergy, suggesting that the control of Th2 responses is a critical step for the prevention of allergic enteropathy in the intestine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of IL-4 and its associated Th2 responses in the pathogenesis and progression of food allergy.
the mechanisms underlying the development of food allergies, and in particular the role of IL-4 and Th2 responses in the development and progression of intestinal damages.
the mechanisms underlying the development and control of allergic responses, especially in the gastrointestinal tract, and the role of IL-4 in the regulation of the mucosal immune responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the lack of IL- 4 in mice sensitized to peanut proteins modulates gut mucosal responses through diminished expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and increased Th1/Th2 cytokines and regulatory cytokines, thereby demonstrating their relevance in controlling allergic inflammatory processes in the gut.
the absence of IL-4 in mice leads to the development of a Th1 response that is associated with the control of intestinal inflammation in food allergy.
IL-4 regulates susceptibility in murine food allergies through a mechanism dependent on intestinal Th2/Th1 balance and the control of inflammatory cytokines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Th2 cytokines are essential for the development of intestinal pathology during food allergy, and that IL-4 is the key cytokine involved in the regulation of the inflammatory response in the gut.

IL-4 is required for the development of intestinal inflammation in food allergy and that IL-4-dependent responses are involved in the regulation of intestinal inflammation through the control of TNF-alpha and Th1/Th2 cytokines.
IL-4 regulates susceptibility and severity of food allergy through the control of intestinal inflammatory responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IL-4 regulates intestinal inflammation in food allergy.
Th2 cytokines, particularly IL-4, are important in the development of gut mucosal inflammation in murine model of food allergy.
IL-4 plays a key role in the development and progression of allergic responses in the intestine.
